question: To reduce the risk of tiredness on a long journey, the Highway Code recommends taking a break of at least how long after every two hours of driving?
options: 45 minutes
5 minutes
30 minutes
15 minutes
explanation: Driving when you are tired greatly increases your risk of collision. To minimise this risk: do not begin a journey if you are tired; plan your journey to take sufficient breaks (a minimum break of at least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving is recommended); if you feel sleepy, stop in a safe place. (Highway Code rule 91.)

question: You start to feel sleepy while driving on a road with no immediate exit. What should you do?
options: Open a window and turn the radio up
Increase speed to finish the journey sooner
Stop in a safe place as soon as possible
Follow the vehicle in front more closely so you concentrate
explanation: Driving when you are tired greatly increases your risk of collision. To minimise this risk: do not begin a journey if you are tired; plan your journey to take sufficient breaks (a minimum break of at least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving is recommended); if you feel sleepy, stop in a safe place. question: You are dazzled by bright sunlight while driving. What should you do?
options: Flash your headlights at oncoming traffic
Pull down the sun visor and continue at the same speed
Speed up to get past the glare
Slow down and, if necessary, stop
explanation: Slow down, and if necessary stop, if you are dazzled by bright sunlight. (Highway Code rule 93.)

question: Before setting off on a journey, what should you do?
options: Plan to use your phone for directions while driving
Plan your route, allow enough time and adjust mirrors and seat for full control
Wear loose footwear so your feet stay relaxed
Wait until you join a main road before adjusting your mirrors
explanation: Before setting off you should ensure that you have planned your route and allowed sufficient time, that clothing and footwear do not prevent you using the controls correctly, and that mirrors and seat are adjusted to ensure comfort, full control and maximum vision. (Highway Code rule 97.)

question: A police vehicle behind you flashes its blue lights and headlights. What must you do?
options: Stop immediately, even at a junction
Speed up so they can follow you to a safer place
Continue to the next service area
Pull over and stop as soon as it is safe to do so
explanation: Police stopping procedures. If the police want to stop your vehicle they will, where possible, attract your attention by flashing blue lights, headlights or sounding their siren or horn, usually from behind. You MUST then pull over and stop as soon as it is safe to do so. (Highway Code rule 106.)

question: A DVSA officer in a marked vehicle flashes amber lights and signals you to follow. What should you do?
options: Follow their directions and stop in the place they indicate
Ignore them — only the police can stop you
Drive to the nearest police station
Stop immediately in the road
explanation: DVSA officers have the power to stop vehicles on all roads. They will attract your attention by flashing amber lights either from the front requesting you to follow them to a safe place to stop, or from behind directing you to pull over to the side. (Highway Code rule 107.)

question: Which of these does the Highway Code list as a distraction you should avoid while driving?
options: Checking your mirrors frequently
Arguing with your passengers or other road users
Listening to traffic reports
Looking far ahead along the road
explanation: Safe driving and riding needs concentration. Avoid distractions when driving or riding such as loud music, reading maps, eating and drinking, and arguing with your passengers or other road users. (Highway Code rule 148.)

question: When may you use a hand-held mobile phone while driving?
options: When driving below 20 mph
When stopped at traffic lights
Only to call 999 or 112 in a genuine emergency when it is unsafe or impractical to stop
When using it as a sat-nav
explanation: You MUST exercise proper control of your vehicle at all times. You MUST NOT use a hand-held mobile phone or similar device when driving or supervising a learner driver, except to call 999 or 112 in a genuine emergency when it is unsafe or impractical to stop. (Highway Code rule 149.)

question: You are supervising a learner driver. May you use a hand-held mobile phone?
options: Yes, but only on dual carriageways
Yes, because you are not driving
Yes, but only for short calls
No — the same restrictions apply as if you were driving
explanation: You MUST exercise proper control of your vehicle at all times. You MUST NOT use a hand-held mobile phone or similar device when driving or supervising a learner driver, except to call 999 or 112 in a genuine emergency when it is unsafe or impractical to stop. (Highway Code rule 149.)

question: Before moving off from the side of the road you should look round to check the blind spots. Why?
options: It warms your neck muscles
It is required by your insurer
To check your seat belt is fastened
Mirrors do not cover every area around the vehicle
explanation: Before moving off you should use all mirrors to check the road is clear, look round to check the blind spots, signal if necessary before moving out, and look round for a final check. Move off only when it is safe to do so. (Highway Code rule 159.)

question: When should you use your mirrors?
options: Only on motorways
Only before overtaking
Frequently, and in good time before signalling, changing direction or speed
Once every minute regardless of conditions
explanation: Mirrors. All mirrors should be used effectively throughout your journey. You should use your mirrors frequently so that you always know what is behind and to each side of you, and use them in good time before you signal or change direction or speed. (Highway Code rule 161.)

question: You start to feel drowsy on a motorway. What should you do?
options: Drive faster to reach your destination sooner
Stop on the hard shoulder for a rest
Leave at the next exit or service area and take a break
Open the window and turn up the radio
explanation: The monotony of driving on a motorway can make you feel sleepy. To minimise the risk, take a break of at least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving. If you feel sleepy, leave the motorway at the next exit or service area. (Highway Code rule 262.)

question: Highway Code rule 254 is about “motorways”. Which statement is taken from this rule?
options: Traffic on motorways usually travels faster than on other roads, so you have less time to react.
